<img src="img/perso.jpeg" alt="Alexandre Marchal" class="profile-photo"/>

My research revolves around a single object: the **genetic covariance matrix**, which describes how phenotypes co-vary across traits and environments through inheritance, and how individuals resemble each other, whether through pedigree, markers or, more recently, learned representations.
I develop **statistical methods** to estimate it when it becomes large and complex, and I use it to understand **how phenotypes are built**: phenotypic plasticity, trade-offs between traits, components of heterosis.
This places my work at the interface of quantitative genetics, statistical modeling and machine learning.

### Main contributions

- **Differentiable REML on GPU.** I developed [pyreml]{.pyreml}, a mixed model library that fits REML by direct differentiation of its loss in `PyTorch`. Running on GPU, it outperforms the state-of-the-art mixed model solver `Wombat` on a dense GBLUP benchmark. Its differentiable design makes it a building block for further developments such as mixed effects neural networks.

- **Factor-analytic mixed models.** With a Master’s student I supervised, I developed a Bayesian implementation of the FA model, then integrated a frequentist version in [pyreml]{.pyreml}: as far as I know, the first open-source REML implementation of the FA mixed model. We illustrated, as a proof of concept, that the kinship can be replaced by a similarity built from neural network embeddings, opening variance decomposition to non-genetic applications (text, images, etc.).

- **Phenotypic plasticity and heterosis.** Using Bayesian random regression along a water-availability gradient, I demonstrated that hybrid larch heterosis, individual genetic contrasts and a growth–density trade-off were all amplified under favorable environmental conditions.

- **Multivariate genetic models.** During my MSc internship, I showed that modeling two correlated yield components jointly improved oil palm selection accuracy, even without the extreme heritability or missing-data patterns usually invoked to justify multivariate models. For hybrid larch, I fitted a 6-trait Bayesian model and characterized the marginal priors induced by parameter expansion, which had not been assessed before.

### Trajectory

After a PhD in quantitative genetics at INRAE-Orléans (2014–2018), I spent ~5 years in the genomic breeding industry and 3 years as a data science consultant.
I then returned to academia as a post-doc researcher at [IGMM — CNRS](https://www.igmm.cnrs.fr/en/team/ai-for-genome-interpretation/), where I work on integrating mixed model concepts into neural network models for genomic prediction.

I have taught **500+** hours of statistics and genetics, including **128** hours at University, the rest to public research institutes and breeding teams.
